title: Knaster-Tarski Fixed-Point Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every monotone function on a complete lattice has a fixed point, and its fixed points form a complete lattice.
short: Monotone self-maps cannot avoid fixed points.
long: Monotone self-maps cannot avoid fixed points. The least fixed point is the infimum of all pre-fixed points.
proof: Take the infimum of the set of x with f(x)<=x and use monotonicity to show it is fixed.
consequence: It justifies least fixed-point semantics and closure constructions.

title: Galois Connections Between Posets
subject: Combinatorics
statement: An adjoint pair of monotone maps between posets satisfies f(x)<=y exactly when x<=g(y); the composites are closure operators.
short: Adjoints translate inequalities across two worlds.
long: Adjoints translate inequalities across two worlds. Every closure operator arises from such a connection in a standard way.
proof: Apply the adjunction twice to show x<=g(f(x)) and f(g(y))<=y, giving idempotent composites.
consequence: Galois connections appear in algebra, topology, and logic.

title: Mobius Function of the Partition Lattice
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For the lattice of set partitions ordered by refinement, the Mobius function from the bottom element to a partition is the product over blocks of (-1) to the block size minus one times the factorial of block size minus one.
short: Each block contributes an independent sign and factorial.
long: Each block contributes an independent sign and factorial. For the one-block partition this recovers the inclusion-exclusion count of surjections.
proof: Use the crosscut theorem or compute by induction on the number of blocks.
consequence: It supports Mobius inversion on partition lattices.

title: Sauer-Shelah Lemma on VC Dimension
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A family of subsets of an n-element set with VC dimension at most d has size at most the sum over i up to d of C(n,i).
short: Low shattering dimension limits family size polynomially.
long: Low shattering dimension limits family size polynomially. The bound is attained by all subsets of size at most d.
proof: Induct on n and d by splitting the family according to whether sets contain a fixed element.
consequence: It is the combinatorial foundation of statistical learning theory.

title: Union-Closed Sets Conjecture
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Open: every finite union-closed family of sets other than the trivial family has an element belonging to at least half of its members.
short: An element should appear in at least half the sets.
long: An element should appear in at least half the sets. The conjecture remains open in general, though it is known for families with small sets and for many lattice cases.
proof: Open. No general proof is known; partial results use lattice theory and compressor arguments.
consequence: It is a famously simple-looking open problem in extremal set theory.

title: Tree Characterization by Edge Count
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A connected graph on n vertices is a tree if and only if it has exactly n-1 edges.
short: A tree is a minimally connected graph.
long: A tree is a minimally connected graph. Any connected graph has a spanning tree, and extra edges create cycles.
proof: Remove cycle edges until acyclic; the resulting spanning tree has n-1 edges by induction.
consequence: It gives a quick test for tree structure.

title: Every Tree Has at Least Two Leaves
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Every tree with at least two vertices has at least two vertices of degree one.
short: The ends of a longest path are leaves.
long: The ends of a longest path are leaves. A single-vertex tree is the only tree without a degree-one vertex.
proof: Take a longest path; if an endpoint had another neighbour, the path could be extended or would create a cycle.
consequence: Leaf existence supports pruning algorithms and tree induction.

title: Prufer Sequence Bijection for Labelled Trees
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Labelled trees on n vertices biject with sequences of length n-2 over the label set.
short: Repeatedly delete the smallest leaf to encode a tree.
long: Repeatedly delete the smallest leaf to encode a tree. The decoding algorithm reconstructs the tree by joining each sequence entry to the smallest absent label.
proof: Leaf deletion and its reverse are inverse maps, giving the bijection and Cayley's count.
consequence: It yields Cayley's formula and useful random-tree models.

title: Forest Edge Count by Components
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A forest with n vertices and c connected components has exactly n-c edges.
short: Each tree component with v_i vertices has v_i-1 edges.
long: Each tree component with v_i vertices has v_i-1 edges. Summing over components gives n minus the number of components.
proof: Apply the tree edge count to each component and sum.
consequence: It generalizes the tree edge count and tracks component changes.

title: Dimension of the Cycle Space
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The cycle space of a graph with n vertices, m edges, and c components has dimension m-n+c over the two-element field.
short: Each independent cycle adds one degree of freedom.
long: Each independent cycle adds one degree of freedom. It is also called the cyclomatic number or first Betti number of the graph.
proof: A spanning forest has n-c edges; each remaining edge creates one independent fundamental cycle.
consequence: It links graph theory with homology and network analysis.

title: Cut Space Is Orthogonal to Cycle Space
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Over the two-element field, every edge cut vector has even intersection with every cycle vector.
short: A cycle crosses any cut an even number of times.
long: A cycle crosses any cut an even number of times. This orthogonality explains the decomposition of the edge space into cut and cycle parts.
proof: Travel around a cycle; each time it crosses the cut it must later cross back.
consequence: It is the graph-theoretic basis of Kirchhoff's circuit laws.

title: Planar Graph Edge Bound for Simple Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A simple planar graph with n at least 3 has at most 3n-6 edges, and a triangle-free planar graph has at most 2n-4 edges.
short: Euler's formula and face lengths limit density.
long: Euler's formula and face lengths limit density. Equality holds for triangulations and for quadrangulations respectively.
proof: Each face has length at least 3, or 4 in the triangle-free case, and each edge borders two face sides.
consequence: It quickly proves nonplanarity of dense graphs.

title: Nonplanarity of K5 and K3,3
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The complete graph K5 and the complete bipartite graph K3,3 are not planar.
short: Both violate the planar edge or face-length bounds.
long: Both violate the planar edge or face-length bounds. K5 has too many edges, while K3,3 is bipartite with too many edges for a quadrangulation.
proof: Apply m<=3n-6 to K5 and m<=2n-4 to K3,3.
consequence: They are the two forbidden building blocks in Kuratowski's theorem.

title: Kuratowski's Planarity Criterion
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A finite graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K5 or K3,3.
short: Planarity is characterized by two forbidden topological subgraphs.
long: Planarity is characterized by two forbidden topological subgraphs. A subdivision replaces edges by internally disjoint paths.
proof: The hard direction analyzes a minimal nonplanar graph and reconstructs a subdivision.
consequence: It gives a structural, although not efficient, planarity test.

title: Wagner's Minor Criterion for Planarity
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A finite graph is planar if and only if it has neither K5 nor K3,3 as a minor.
short: Forbidden minors characterize planarity.
long: Forbidden minors characterize planarity. Unlike subdivisions, minors allow contracting edges as well as deleting them.
proof: Kuratowski's subdivisions yield minors, and the converse follows by analyzing minor-minimal obstructions.
consequence: It is a precursor to the general graph minor theory.

title: Dirac's Minimum-Degree Hamiltonicity Condition
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A simple graph on n at least 3 vertices with minimum degree at least n/2 contains a Hamiltonian cycle.
short: Large minimum degree forces a spanning cycle.
long: Large minimum degree forces a spanning cycle. The bound is sharp: two cliques sharing one vertex fail just below it.
proof: Take a longest path; its endpoints have neighbours on the path that allow insertion into a cycle through all vertices.
consequence: It is the first major sufficient condition for Hamiltonicity.

title: Ore's Degree-Sum Hamiltonicity Condition
subject: Graph Theory
statement: If every pair of nonadjacent vertices in an n-vertex simple graph has degree sum at least n, then the graph is Hamiltonian.
short: Nonedges cannot have too small combined degree.
long: Nonedges cannot have too small combined degree. Dirac's condition implies Ore's condition.
proof: Close the graph by repeatedly adding edges between nonadjacent pairs of degree sum at least n until it is complete or Hamiltonian.
consequence: It generalizes Dirac's theorem.

title: Chvatal-Erdos Connectivity Condition
subject: Graph Theory
statement: If the vertex connectivity of a graph is at least its independence number, then the graph is Hamiltonian.
short: Connectivity that dominates independence forces a spanning cycle.
long: Connectivity that dominates independence forces a spanning cycle. It applies to many dense graphs with limited independent sets.
proof: A longest cycle leaving vertices outside yields an independent set whose size exceeds connectivity, a contradiction.
consequence: It links three fundamental graph invariants.

title: Bondy-Chvatal Closure
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Adding an edge between nonadjacent vertices whose degree sum is at least n preserves Hamiltonicity.
latex: d(u)+d(v)\ge n\Rightarrow G+uv\text{ Hamiltonian iff }G\text{ is}
short: Degree-sum closure changes no Hamiltonicity information.
long: Degree-sum closure changes no Hamiltonicity information. The iterative closure is unique and decides Hamiltonicity in some graph classes.
proof: If a Hamiltonian cycle uses the new edge, the degree-sum condition inserts u and v into a spanning path of the original graph.
consequence: It unifies Ore-type arguments.

title: Grotzsch's Three-Colour Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Every triangle-free planar graph is 3-colourable.
short: Removing triangles improves the planar colour bound.
long: Removing triangles improves the planar colour bound. It cannot be extended to nonplanar triangle-free graphs, which may have arbitrarily large chromatic number.
proof: A minimal counterexample is shown to be critical; discharging rules give a contradiction.
consequence: It refines the Four Colour Theorem in the triangle-free case.

title: Brooks' Colouring Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A connected graph with maximum degree Delta has chromatic number at most Delta unless it is a complete graph or an odd cycle.
short: Greedy colouring is almost optimal.
long: Greedy colouring is almost optimal. The exceptions require Delta+1 colours only for cliques and odd cycles.
proof: Order vertices suitably and greedily colour; connected non-exception graphs admit a spanning order where each vertex has a later neighbour.
consequence: It sharpens the trivial greedy bound.

title: Five Colour Theorem for Planar Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Every planar graph can be coloured with five colours.
short: Kempe chains give a simple inductive colouring.
long: Kempe chains give a simple inductive colouring. It is weaker than the Four Colour Theorem but much easier to prove.
proof: In a minimal counterexample, find a vertex of degree at most five and recolour using Kempe chains.
consequence: It was the classical stepping stone to the Four Colour Theorem.

title: Perfect Graph Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A graph is perfect exactly when its complement is perfect.
short: Perfection is inherited by complements.
long: Perfection is inherited by complements. In a perfect graph every induced subgraph has chromatic number equal to clique number.
proof: Lovasz proved the replication lemma and used it to establish complement invariance.
consequence: It explains symmetry between clique covers and colourings.

title: Strong Perfect Graph Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A graph is perfect if and only if it has no induced odd cycle of length at least five and no complement of such a cycle.
latex: G\text{ perfect}\iff\text{no odd holes or antiholes}
short: Odd holes and their complements are the only obstructions.
long: Odd holes and their complements are the only obstructions. The result resolved a long-standing conjecture of Berge.
proof: Chudnovsky, Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas gave a structural proof using decomposition of imperfect graphs.
consequence: It characterizes perfection by a list of forbidden induced subgraphs.

title: Koning's Matching-Vertex-Cover Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: In a bipartite graph, the maximum matching size equals the minimum vertex cover size.
short: Bipartite matchings and covers are dual.
long: Bipartite matchings and covers are dual. It fails for general graphs, where only the inequality nu <= tau holds.
proof: Use alternating paths from unmatched vertices to construct a cover of size equal to the matching.
consequence: It is the graph analogue of linear programming duality.
